Rules: real_exam/TEACHING_STYLE_GUIDE.md R1-R35 (no 'which way is better' verdict) + NITZAN_RHYTHM_DELIVERY.md P1-P13. Calm preset on the question reading and plain calculations.

slides.say: Ninety stickers are shared among twenty-six children, and every child gets at least three stickers. Which number cannot be the number of children who get exactly three stickers?

This is the same type as the apple baskets, with new numbers. I promised a shortcut, and here it is. [short pause] We'll solve it in three different ways, by counting the spare stickers, by looking at the ends of the range, and by checking the edge cases.

[short pause] Let's start with the spare stickers. First we fill every child up to the minimum, three each. To get twenty-six times three, we take twenty times three, which is sixty. Then we add six times three, which is eighteen. Sixty plus eighteen is seventy-eight stickers.
Ninety minus seventy-eight leaves twelve spare stickers.

A child gets more than three only if at least one spare sticker goes to that child. Twelve spares can lift at most twelve children. So at least twenty-six minus twelve, fourteen children get exactly three.
Thirteen is less than fourteen, so thirteen is impossible. Choice number two is our answer.
at: Choice number two is our answer

slides.say: [pause] Now by looking at the ends of the range. The smallest count is fourteen, as the spares showed. The biggest is twenty-five. Twenty-five children get three each, that's seventy-five, and the last child gets ninety minus seventy-five, fifteen. All twenty-six can't get three, because that's only seventy-eight.

And every count in between works too. Why is that? Because each spare sticker lifts one child, and moving one sticker changes the count by exactly one. So the count steps from fourteen up to twenty-five, one at a time, with no holes.

When the count changes by one at a time, the range has no holes. Then three choices are inside the range, and the impossible one must be at an end. In order, the choices are thirteen, fourteen, seventeen and twenty. So only thirteen or twenty can be outside.

One check decides. Twenty children with three is sixty stickers. Thirty are left for the other six children, five each, more than three. So twenty works, and thirteen is the impossible one. Choice number two is our answer.
at: Choice number two is our answer

slides.say: But careful, this is not a general rule. Remember the chip with two and six. Its totals jumped by four, fourteen, eighteen, twenty-two, and there were holes. Fixed jumps leave holes. There are no holes only when the value can move by one.

[pause] Now the edge cases, a very easy calculation at the edge. Here too the count moves by one, so the impossible choice is at one end. What if every child gets exactly three? Twenty-six times three is seventy-eight, and we need ninety. So twenty-six doesn't work.
Now one child fewer at three. Twenty-five children with three is seventy-five, and the last child takes fifteen. That works, so twenty-five is the top of the range.

Our choices twenty, seventeen and fourteen are all below twenty-five, so the top end is no problem. The impossible one must be at the bottom, the smallest choice, thirteen. Choice number two is our answer, and I'll see you in the next question.
at: Choice number two is our answer
